title: How to debug Burst
sub: Is the bug in the logic, the threads or Burst; how to set a breakpoint, what to log, and how to measure speed
cards/0/title: First find out whether it’s Burst
cards/0/body:
Debugging a Burst job is two different tasks: a wrong result and too slow. Let’s start with the first.

The first question is whether Burst or your logic is to blame. Turn off Jobs > Burst > Enable Compilation: jobs run as plain C#, and the usual managed breakpoints work. The bug is still there — it’s in the logic, hunt it down the usual way. It’s gone — look at what behaves differently under Burst: a false [NoAlias], fields with [NativeDisableContainerSafetyRestriction], FloatMode.Fast.

You don’t always have to turn everything off: put a managed breakpoint into Burst code with a debugger attached, and Unity disables Burst for that code path by itself, and turns it back on once you remove the breakpoints.

A trap: in the Editor Burst compiles in the background, and the first frames may run managed code. For a Burst-vs-managed comparison and for measurements, wait for the compilation: [BurstCompile(CompileSynchronously = true)] on the job or Jobs > Burst > Synchronous Compilation. In a build it doesn’t matter — there Burst is always compiled ahead of time.
cards/1/title: All jobs on the main thread
cards/1/body:
The second question is whether the threads are to blame. Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Use Job Threads: untick it, and every job runs on the main thread right when it’s scheduled. No more parallelism, the order is exactly the order of Schedule(), and breakpoints fire predictably.

The same from code is JobsUtility.JobWorkerCount = 0, and back to automatic is JobsUtility.ResetJobWorkerCount(). After an Editor restart Use Job Threads is on again.

For a single job, Run() is simpler: the same Execute, the same Burst code, but here and now on the current thread.

How to read the result: the bug is gone without threads — so it’s a race or a missing dependency between jobs. With one thread they just happened to run in the “right” order, which nothing guaranteed once threads were involved.
cards/2/q: A job’s result is sometimes garbage. With Use Job Threads off, the bug never reproduces. Where do you look?
cards/2/options/0: For a race or a missing dependency between jobs: without threads they run strictly in Schedule() order
cards/2/options/1: In Burst: it miscompiles the job, so Enable Compilation should stay off for good
cards/2/options/2: For a memory leak: Leak Detection will show where
cards/2/options/3: At FloatMode.Fast: it doesn’t apply with one thread
cards/2/explain: Use Job Threads removes exactly one thing — parallelism. If the bug is gone without it, two jobs touch the same data with no dependency (or with safety switched off). Find who writes and who reads, and link them with dependsOn.
cards/2/wrong/1: Burst is the same in both cases; only the parallelism changed.
cards/2/wrong/2: A leak doesn’t corrupt results — it’s about memory that wasn’t freed.
cards/2/wrong/3: The float mode is a property of the compiled code; it doesn’t depend on the number of threads.
cards/3/body:
If the bug exists only under Burst, you debug the Burst code itself with a native debugger.

Jobs > Burst > Native Debug Mode Compilation turns off optimizations for all Burst code — handy for debugging, but everything gets slower. For one job, use [BurstCompile(Debug = true)]: no optimizations and with debug info; builds respect this flag too. It doesn’t stay in a release.

Then attach a native debugger — Visual Studio, Xcode — to the Editor or to the build, and set breakpoints in the job’s C# source. A build needs symbols: Development Build or Force Debug Information in the Burst AOT settings; they sit next to lib_burst_generated. A breakpoint in code is supported too — System.Diagnostics.Debugger.Break() — but the debugger’s conditional breakpoints are more convenient.
cards/4/body:
You can log from Burst, but not the way you do in ordinary C#. Debug.Log, Debug.LogWarning and Debug.LogError take a literal or an interpolated $"..." string (and string.Format with a literal format).

The arguments are built-in value types (int, float, bool, double…) and Unity.Mathematics vectors such as float3. Your own struct’s ToString() won’t work — it prints the type name. You can’t concatenate strings with +, pass a string to your own method or keep it in a field — for text in fields there’s FixedString64Bytes and its relatives.

[BurstDiscard] drops a method from Burst compilation: under Burst the call simply does nothing, and in managed mode the method runs and can touch anything. Such a method can’t return a value.

And a practical point: a log in the Execute of a parallel job over 100,000 elements is 100,000 messages. Log one index, or behind a condition.
cards/5/q: Which calls compile in a Burst job? Pick all that apply.
cards/5/options/0: Debug.Log($"i={i} pos={p}"), where i is an int and p is a float3
cards/5/options/1: Debug.Log("hp: " + hp), where hp is a float
cards/5/options/3: Debug.Log(name), where name is a string field of the job struct
cards/5/explain: A literal and an interpolation with primitives and Mathematics vectors are supported. Concatenation with + isn’t: the format has to be a literal. And a string field in a job is impossible in the first place: Burst doesn’t allow strings in struct fields; that’s what FixedString is for.
cards/6/title: throw and safety checks: Editor vs build
cards/6/body:
An exception from Burst code is caught in the Editor and printed to the console — the game goes on. In a build, any throw in Burst is an abort: the application crashes. Burst warns about this (BC1370).

That’s why checks with throw go into a method marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")]: such methods and their calls don’t make it into the build. Write the attribute in full — System.Diagnostics.Conditional: a using System.Diagnostics next to UnityEngine makes Debug ambiguous.

Safety checks — out-of-bounds container access, writes to [ReadOnly], races — exist only in the Editor. Jobs > Burst > Enable Safety Checks (Off / On / Force On) controls the checks inside Burst code; Force On turns them on even where DisableSafetyChecks = true is set; after an Editor reload it is On again. The Job System’s own checks are Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Enable Jobs Debugger. In builds these checks are unavailable, not merely switched off — which is why bugs are reproduced in the Editor.
cards/7/q: The game crashes in a build with no message. In the Editor an exception from a Burst job sometimes shows up in the console, but the game keeps running. What is going on?
cards/7/options/0: In the Editor an exception from Burst is caught and logged, while in a build a throw is an abort; find the cause from the Editor exception and wrap the checks in Conditional
cards/7/options/1: Safety checks are off by default in builds — turn them on in Player Settings
cards/7/options/2: Burst ignores throw in builds, so something else is crashing
cards/7/options/3: It’s a memory leak that builds up in the build until it crashes
cards/7/explain: The same exception looks like a console line in the Editor and like a crash in a build. You look for the cause where it’s visible: in the Editor with Safety Checks. And the checks with throw go into methods marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")], so they stay out of the build.
cards/7/wrong/1: These checks are unavailable in builds; there is nothing to “turn on” in Player Settings.
cards/7/wrong/2: The opposite: an unwrapped throw stays in the build and crashes the application.
cards/7/wrong/3: A leak is shown by Leak Detection, and it doesn’t look like an exception from a job in the Editor console.
cards/8/body:
A native container nobody freed is a leak of unmanaged memory. Leak Detection finds it: Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Leak Detection Level, or NativeLeakDetection.Mode from code.

Enabled (the default in the Editor and development builds) only counts leaks and reports the number at domain unload. Enabled With Stack Trace shows where each unfreed allocation was made — that’s what you want when hunting, but allocations get more expensive, so it’s turned on temporarily. Disabled is the default in regular builds.

The most common cause is an Allocator.Persistent allocation made in Awake with no Dispose() in OnDestroy.
cards/9/q: A Burst job sometimes gives a wrong result. Put the debugging steps in order.
cards/9/items/0: Reproduce in the Editor with Enable Safety Checks and Enable Jobs Debugger
cards/9/items/1: Narrow it down: turn off Use Job Threads, then Enable Compilation
cards/9/items/2: Find the spot: a breakpoint in managed mode, or Debug.Log
cards/9/items/3: If the bug exists only under Burst: Native Debug Mode Compilation and a native debugger
cards/9/items/4: Fix it and check in a build
cards/9/explain: First give the checks a chance: a safety exception often names the cause right away. Then narrow it down — threads or Burst. Then find the line the cheapest way. The native debugger is for a bug that lives only in Burst code. And check in a build, where there are no checks.
cards/10/title: Debugging speed: the Profiler and the Burst Inspector
cards/10/body:
For “too slow” the tools are different. The Profiler’s Timeline view shows jobs on worker threads by name, the main thread’s waits, and how busy the threads are. Inside a job you can mark sections: ProfilerMarker works in Burst — new ProfilerMarker("Name") and Auto() or Begin()/End().

The hot loop is examined in the Burst Inspector: packed or scalar, and what blocked vectorization (lesson 1). Jobs > Burst > Show Timings prints how long each job took to compile.

How to measure honestly: in the Editor, the Jobs Debugger and Safety Checks add their own cost — turn them off for a measurement; Burst must already be compiled (Synchronous Compilation or a warm-up); the final numbers come from a build. For a deep dive into a build, Instruments and Superluminal work with the symbols from lib_burst_generated.
cards/11/task: Make ApplyDamageJob safe for a build: move the check with throw into static void CheckIndex(int index, int length) marked [System.Diagnostics.Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")], and call it from Execute. Execute itself must have no throw. Rewrite the log with an interpolated $"..." string, without concatenation.
cards/11/checks/0/label: CheckIndex is a static void with [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")]
cards/11/checks/4/label: Debug.Log is called with an interpolated $"..."
cards/11/checks/5/label: Debug.Log has no string concatenation with +
cards/11/explain: In the Editor CheckIndex runs and throws a clear exception that Burst shows in the console. In a build the method and its call are gone, so there is no abort either. String concatenation doesn’t compile in Burst; interpolation with a float does. The attribute is written in full because a using System.Diagnostics next to UnityEngine would make Debug ambiguous.
cards/12/q: Interviewer: “In the Editor your Burst job is slower than promised. What do you check before drawing conclusions?”
cards/12/options/0: That I’m measuring already compiled Burst without extra checks: wait for compilation, turn off the Jobs Debugger and Safety Checks, and take the final measurement in a build
cards/12/options/1: Turn on Native Debug Mode Compilation to see the code more precisely
cards/12/options/2: Add a Debug.Log to Execute to see how many times it runs
cards/12/options/3: Turn off Use Job Threads to remove the threading overhead
cards/12/explain: In the Editor it’s easy to measure the wrong thing: the first frames of managed code before the background compilation finishes, and safety checks on top of Burst. Remove them or measure in a build, and only then look at the Timeline and the Burst Inspector.
cards/12/wrong/1: Native Debug Mode turns optimizations off — the code gets even slower, and the measurement means nothing.
cards/12/wrong/2: A log per element becomes the main workload by itself.
cards/12/wrong/3: Without worker threads the parallelism is gone — that’s a tool for finding races, not for measuring.
